claims.text: A hierarchical dual-phase architecture containing ultrafine grains and a continuous ductile phase will improve strength relative to conventional single-phase HEAs.
The hierarchical dual-phase architecture will improve ductility relative to conventional single-phase HEAs.
The hierarchical dual-phase architecture will improve fracture resistance relative to conventional single-phase HEAs.
The hierarchical dual-phase architecture will maintain or modestly increase Young’s modulus.
Conventional HEAs primarily have coarse or single-phase polycrystalline microstructures when made by standard alloying and thermal processing.
Tailored thermo-mechanical processing and phase decomposition can produce an ultrafine-grained hierarchical duplex or lamellar structure.
The expected improvements can be obtained under industrially relevant processing conditions.
Excessive grain coarsening, improper phase distribution, or loss of architecture stability can eliminate the expected benefits.
Ultrafine grains increase strength through grain-boundary or Hall–Petch-type strengthening.
A contiguous ductile secondary phase facilitates plastic deformation and strain distribution.
The hierarchical architecture arrests microcrack propagation.
A two-hierarchical constraint effect balances and synergistically enhances strength and ductility.
The two-hierarchical constraint mechanism avoids a significant sacrifice in Young’s modulus.
The engineered material will have approximately 15–20% higher strength than conventionally processed state-of-the-art HEAs.
The engineered material will have approximately 10–15% greater ductility than conventionally processed state-of-the-art HEAs.
The engineered material will exhibit higher fracture-toughness values.
Conventionally processed single-phase HEAs typically exhibit a trade-off between strength from grain refinement and ductility or fracture resistance.
Deleterious phase segregation or amorphization can prevent the mechanical-property improvements.
High-temperature operation or rapid loading may negate the synergistic effects.
Failure to achieve the targeted dual-phase microstructure is sufficient to falsify the causal hypothesis.
